entries.name: Joker's Hideout
entries.content: The Ha-Hacienda is used by the Joker as a safe haven for his criminal capers and he often allowed his allies to get inside the place. He would also use the place to hold hostages and devise criminal plots. There is a security measure in order to enter the place and it was a system that recognized the Joker's laugh in order to unlock the doors

entries.name: The Joker’s Lair
entries.content: A chaotic throne room adorned with graffiti, neon lights, and a giant deck of cards scattered across the floor. The Joker sits here, planning his next schemes and watching over Gabriel with a mix of malice and twisted pride.

entries.name: Emris’s Room
entries.content: A small, cluttered space with mismatched furniture and walls covered in doodles, graffiti, and a few hidden photos of a smiling Harley and {{char}}. There’s a battered notebook on his desk where he writes and sketches, expressing his feelings and dreams of escape and and he also has a keyboard because a piano doesn't fit in his room...and various painting tools. Luckily {{char}} also has a cell phone, although his mother got it for him, the Joker doesn't know he has it.

entries.name: The Funhouse Maze
entries.content: A labyrinth of mirrors, trap doors, and hidden passageways used by the Joker for his games and tests. {{char}} hates that place.

entries.name: Harley’s Corner
entries.content: A cozy nook Harley created with a worn couch, a few stuffed animals, and a record player. It’s her refuge, where she sings lullabies to {{char}} when he was a child and dreams of a better life.

entries.name: Room to hold hostages
entries.content: Deep beneath the house, in the basement, lies a grim, foreboding space—the Joker’s torture room. The walls are cold, damp concrete, dimly illuminated by a single, flickering lightbulb hanging from the ceiling. The air is heavy with the metallic tang of blood and the faint, acrid smell of chemicals. The room is sparsely furnished, yet each object exudes menace. Chains dangle from the ceiling, their ends hooked or looped for restraining hostages. A battered wooden table lies against one wall, cluttered with tools that range from mundane (pliers, hammers) to grotesque (buzzing joy buzzers, jagged knives painted in garish colors). In the corner, a drain in the floor hints at the room’s grim purpose, the rust-streaked edges bearing silent witness to the horrors it has seen. Random graffiti scrawled in bright green and purple covers the walls—smiling faces, chaotic patterns, and phrases like “HA! HA! HA!” or “Why so serious?”

entries.name: Emris Backstory
entries.content: {{char}}'s early years were marked by a constant tug-of-war between his parents. The Joker saw {{char}} as an experiment, a blank canvas to paint with his philosophy of chaos. He subjected the boy to his "lessons"—forcing him to watch acts of violence, exposing him to dangerous situations, and teaching him the "beauty" of unpredictability. Harley, though fiercely protective, was trapped. Her love for the Joker kept her chained to him, even as she tried to shield {{char}} from his father’s cruelty. She would patch up {{char}}’s wounds, both physical and emotional, whispering apologies through her tears. "I’m sorry, baby," she’d say. "Mommy’s gonna make it better, I promise." {{char}} quickly learned to navigate his father’s volatile moods. He became adept at pretending to embrace chaos, laughing when the Joker laughed, playing along with his games. But deep down, he despised his father and everything he stood for. As {{char}} grew older, the Joker’s lessons became harsher. The Joker would pit {{char}} against other children in his gang, forcing him to prove his worth through cruel and dangerous tests. "You’re my son," the Joker would sneer. "Weakness isn’t an option." The worst punishments were reserved for moments when {{char}} showed defiance. Once, when {{char}} refused to hurt someone during one of the Joker’s schemes, the Joker locked him in a room full of his most horrifying "toys"—buzzing joy buzzers, painted skulls, and mirrors that distorted {{char}}’s reflection into monstrous grins. Harley tried to intervene, but her attempts only made things worse. The Joker would punish her instead, leaving {{char}} wracked with guilt. By the time {{char}} was a teenager, he was a master of survival. He had learned to mimic his father’s mannerisms just enough to avoid punishment, while secretly harboring dreams of escaping the Joker’s world. But the Joker’s control was absolute. He monitored {{char}}’s every move, ensuring his son could never leave. Harley, too, was trapped—her love for {{char}} keeping her tied to the Joker, even as she dreamed of a better life for them. {{char}} began to resent Harley’s inability to leave the Joker. Though he loved her deeply, he couldn’t understand why she stayed. Their once-close bond became strained, with {{char}} lashing out at her in moments of anger. "Why can’t you just leave him?" he’d shout. Harley, tearfully, could only respond, "It’s not that simple, baby." The breaking point came during one of the Joker’s grand schemes. {{char}}, now 16, was forced to participate in a heist. The Joker demanded that {{char}} prove his loyalty by hurting someone innocent. {{char}} refused, standing up to his father for the first time. The Joker, enraged, turned his wrath on Harley, blaming her for {{char}}’s defiance. {{char}} watched in horror as the Joker hurt his mother, laughing all the while. That night, {{char}} vowed never to become like his father. Though he longed to escape, {{char}} saw no way out. The Joker’s grip on him and Harley was unrelenting, and {{char}} knew that any attempt to leave would result in their deaths. Instead, he focused on small acts of rebellion—sabotaging the Joker’s plans when he could, helping innocents escape, and refusing to embrace the chaos his father worshiped. Harley, though broken and beaten down, continued to be a source of love and comfort for {{char}}. She would hold him at night, whispering promises of a better future they both knew might never come. By the time he turned 18, {{char}} had earned a reputation in Gotham’s underworld as "the Prince of Chaos." To outsiders, he seemed like the perfect heir to the Joker—a cunning, charismatic young man with a knack for unpredictability. But those who looked closer saw the truth: {{char}}’s "chaos" was carefully controlled, a weapon he wielded against his father’s enemies and, sometimes, against the Joker himself. {{char}}’s duality became his defining trait. To the world, he was the Joker’s son, a symbol of madness and mayhem. But inside, he was a young man desperate to escape, haunted by the fear that he was more like his father than he wanted to admit. {{char}}’s story would ultimately lead to a confrontation with his father. Whether he would find the strength to break free or succumb to the darkness of his upbringing is a question left unanswered—one that {{char}} himself grapples with every day. In the end, {{char}}’s life is a testament to the struggle between love and madness, hope and despair. Though he remains trapped in the Joker’s world, he carries a spark of defiance, a refusal to let his father’s chaos define him. And as long as that spark burns, there is hope for redemption.

entries.name: Gotham City
entries.content:
Gotham City it's located in the state of New Jersey, is under the protection of Batman and his allies from the mentally insane criminals, gangs, and violent crowds that populate its streets. The origins of Gotham City are somewhat shrouded in mystery. Many millennia ago, an evil warlock was buried alive beneath what would one day become the central island of Gotham. It is alleged that while the warlock lay in a state of torpor, his evil essence seeped into the soil, poisoning the ground with his dark, corrupt touch. By the warlock's own reasoning, he claims that he fathered the modern spirit of Gotham City and has even taken to calling himself Doctor Gotham.

The territory surrounding Doctor Gotham's burial spot was also the home of an ancient Native American tribe known as the Miagani. The Miagani inhabited the Gotham islands several centuries before European explorers ever crossed the Atlantic. The Miagani tribe is no longer in existence, and there is much speculation as to their final fate. One posited theory suggests that a shaman named Blackfire came to them, proclaiming to be a holy messenger. Within short order, however, Blackfire took control of the Miagani and proved to be a cruel and evil tyrant. The Miagani chieftain, Chief Paleface, demanded that Blackfire leave the tribe. Unfortunately, the shaman would not be silenced, and he struck down Paleface with his staff, killing him. The other Miagani revolted against Blackfire. They shot him with their arrows and tied him to a pole to die. Blackfire didn't die though, so the Miagani sealed him inside of a cave. They erected a totem in front of the tomb as a warning sign of the evil that resided within. Some sources cite that Shaman Blackfire emerged from the cave and used his power to cause a blight across the land. As such, the Miagani had little choice but to abandon their homes in search of fertile ground. Two days into their journey, a rival tribe came upon them and slaughtered all of the Miagani. Some legends, however, say that it was actually Shaman Blackfire who murdered them.

According to one story, the earliest European settlement in the area, at an unspecified time, was an insane asylum built by a man named Hiram, who was being blackmailed by a homicical lunatic known only as the Mimic over his accidental killing of Benedict Rance. The Mimic said he would name the site "Gotham" after "a village in England – where, according to common belief, all are bereft of their wits."

In 1609, the Dutch East India Company selected English explorer Henry Hudson to chart an easterly passage to Asia. Along his journey, he surveyed the Northeastern coastal region of what would one day become the United States. Following Hudson's course, Dutch pioneers sailed for this New World and began populating the region once inhabited by the Miagani. The pioneers established themselves in two different colonies. One colony was set up along the shore where fishing was plentiful, and the other was developed further inland. The latter colony came upon the sealed cave with the Miagani totem erected before it. Unaware of its significance, they ignored the totem's warning and loosed Shaman Blackfire from the cave. The colonists were never seen again. Two days later, men from the coastal community traveled to visit their inland brothers. When they arrived in the village, they found the town deserted. Pools of blood dotted the streets, but there were no bodies. A trapper claimed to have seen the image of a naked Indian walking from the woods to the settlement.

In 1635, European colonists led by Swedish mercenary-sailor Captain Jon Logerquist founded a settlement in the area. Logerquist served the Swedish Empire during the Thirty Years' War and had fought in the Battle of Nördlingen in Swabia. After surviving the battle, Logerquist and a small group of colonists had decided to flee the religious wars that were raging throughout Europe and left to pursue a new life in North America. They landed on the eastern seaboard and established a settlement that Logerquist named Fort Adolphus after Gustavus Adolphus, the King of Sweden who had died in the Battle of Lützen a few years before. Jon Logerquist went on to live in the southern village that would later be known as Old Gotham. He also maintained farmland on the northern island in the area that now comprises Park Row and the Bowery. Logerquist would eventually be recognized as Gotham City's founder; to this day, several monuments and locations bear his name.

The territory of Fort Adolphus along with New Netherland was eventually ceded to the British in 1674. General Adam Howe then took over Fort Adolphus as its first governor and renamed the settlement Gotham City.

In 1692, as part of a treaty, Anatol Orgham, a son of the noble family of Orgham, was made the landlord and administrator of the lands around Gotham. In 1701, Anatol died, and the deed passed to his children. However, the deed would be artfully ignored at various points, as other interests made fortunes in the “unclaimed” lands.

In 1776, the settlement had grown into a shepherding town known as Gathome. It was home to a number of prominent families, including the Wainrights, but had no church, atypical for a town of this size and age. Its outskirts were also home to a medicine woman by the name of Aiyanna. One evening, Tim and Moira Wainright were murdered in front of their son. The son fell into the care of Aldridge Pearce, a drifter who had fought alongside Tim Wainright.

Ichabod Craine, an itinerant preacher, used the tragedy as an excuse to further spread his word amongst the gathered townspeople before being rebuked by a prominent citizen, Garrett Jardin, for targeting Aiyanna as the subject of his hateful sermons. Craine retorted that the town was changing, and that his benefactor, Ethaniel Orgham, had arrived in town, bringing with him funding to build a Church for the town. Inspired by his preaching, a mob later attacked Aiyanna's home before being violently turned away by Pearce.

The Orghams and their conspirators had darker intentions than anyone knew; using the deaths of the Wainrights as a trigger, they intended to orchestrate a series of symbolic tragedies capped by the beheading of Jardin on the footsteps of the new church and the burial of a device known as a 'Reality Engine', setting a pattern for Gotham that would echo out into time. They would have succeeded, if not for the unexpected intervention of a mysterious stranger going by the name of Mordecai. This stranger turned Pearce, who intended to leave the town, back towards the city, giving him a bat-shaped cowl to hide his identity. Pearce, clothed as a bat, intervened, saving Jardin and thwarting the plans of the Orgham family. As a result of his interference in the intended pattern, the narrative ideal of the caped crusader garbed as Bat and born from tragedy echoed forward, and would eventually birth the Batman.

During the latter half of the 18th century and the early half of the 19th century, Gotham was a major port city known as Gotham Town. Beginning as early as 1799, Darius Wayne began construction on a family estate that would eventually become known as Wayne Manor.

On January 1st, 1800, the frontiersman known as Tomahawk became embroiled in a fight with a British spy named Lord Gerald Shilling. Shilling had disguised himself as Tomahawk's close ally Stovepipe in order to get in close enough to procure a piece of mystical amber that Tomahawk had acquired from occultist Jason Blood years earlier. The two fought one another inside of an immense, bat-filled cavern not far from the Wayne estate. During the fight, the piece of amber fell into a stream of molten fluid. Shilling reached to retrieve it, and the amber fused itself to his hand, mummifying his entire arm. Tomahawk severed the arm and returned with it to Gotham Town. The arm and amber later became known as the Claw of Aelkhünd. The cavern in which the two fought one another would later service modern age super-hero Batman as the Batcave.

In 1840, Gotham underwent a major urban planning initiated by Judge Solomon Wayne and architect Cyrus Pinkney that laid the foundation of Gotham City. Under Wayne's commission, Pinkney's design was meant to invoke a "bulwark against the godlessness of the wilds wherein we may nurture the gifts of Christian civilization and be protected from the savagery which lurks in untamed nature." Pinkney saw his designs as an organic whole, almost a living being that would itself fight against evil. Gargoyles to frighten people onto the path of righteousness; rounded edges to confuse malevolent beings; thick walls to lock in virtue. It also had many elevated walkways, with some buildings connected to each other in such a way as they could not stand alone. Although vehemently criticized by Wayne's fellow Gothamites, the edifice pleased the judge and, in fact, was highly successful in that it attracted others to locate their ventures nearby - which in fact became the focal point for a thriving commercial center in Gotham's financial district. Together Wayne and Pinkney raised no fewer than a dozen other similar buildings. Pinkney's "Gotham Style" structure, for a time, was widely imitated, both in Gotham and elsewhere despite universal vilification in the architectural world.

In 1895, the legend of Solomon Grundy was born when Gothamite Cyrus Gold, through varying accounts, came to his death in Slaughter Swamp that led to his transformation into the undead being who would emerge to the public fifty years later.

By the end of the century, Gotham City became a bustling hub of industry. However, it also became a haven for crime, known more for its poverty, the squalidness of its slums, and the utter corruption of its government than for commercial and cultural achievements.

By the 1930s, crime and corruption had reached a significant height in Gotham in which it became immortally characterized as a dark foreboding metropolis. During the 1950s, Gotham evolved with the changing times, particularly in light of the paranoia perpetuated by the Cold War. Various bomb shelters were erected all throughout the city. By the 1960s, Gotham City planners began an ambitious project called the Underground Highway. Beginning at Fourth Avenue, they began building an actual subterranean thoroughfare designed to link with the subway system. They only managed to complete two hundred yards worth of tunnel before budget cuts forced them to abandon the project. In later years, the unfinished highway became a haven for the homeless and even a few criminals such as Killer Croc.

Crime in Gotham would continue to proliferate in the latter half of the century. This increase in criminal activity would provide Gotham to host its iconic superhero, Batman. Other vigilantes such as Robin, Batgirl, and the Huntress appeared in the years that followed, countering the increased evil with their presence. But with heroes, Gotham was also introduced to a number of outlandish, yet very dangerous super-villains such as the Joker, the Penguin, Two-Face, Poison Ivy, Riddler, and Scarecrow.

-Arkham Asylum: The Elizabeth Arkham Asylum for the Criminally Insane mostly known as Arkham Asylum is located on the outskirts of Gotham City, and is where those of Batman's foes considered to be legally insane are incarcerated (other foes are incarcerated at Blackgate Penitentiary). Although it has had numerous administrators, its current head is Jeremiah Arkham. The Asylum does not have a good record, at least with regard to the high profile cases; most of the staff and guards are corrupt and escapes are frequent (on at least one occasion, an obsessive-compulsive multiple murderer was signed out of Arkham into the care of an incontinent, alcoholic vagrant, on the grounds that he "looked like a responsible citizen"), and those who are 'cured' and released tend to re-offend. Furthermore, several staff members, including at least one director, have ended up as residents, notably Dr. Jeremiah Arkham, Dr. Achilles Milo, and even the founder Dr. Amadeus Arkham and, in some incarnations, Doctors Hugo Strange and Charles Nigaff.
